subject: Climate & Environment
title: El Niño and La Niña
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on El Niño and La Niña.

hook.text: Every few years, the Pacific Ocean shifts moods — and the whole world's weather changes with it.

buildup.text: During El Niño, warm water spreads east across the Pacific, altering rainfall and wind patterns.

discovery.text: La Niña does the opposite — cold water dominates, bringing drought to some regions and floods to others.

twist.text: El Niño years are often the hottest on record. 2023 was both an El Niño year and the hottest ever.

climax.text: Climate change is amplifying these swings, making El Niño years hotter and La Niña droughts deeper.

punchline.text: The Pacific's mood swings set the tone for the whole planet.

quiz.question: What happens during an El Niño event?
options: Warm water spreads east across the Pacific

details.summary: El Nino and La Nina are opposite phases of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a natural climate pattern in the tropical Pacific. El Nino warms eastern Pacific surface waters and shifts rainfall patterns globally, while La Nina cools them, often intensifying droughts and floods in different regions.
details.whyItMatters: ENSO events affect weather, agriculture, and disaster risk on every continent. Recognizing these cycles helps governments prepare for floods, droughts, and food shortages.
takeaways: El Nino warms the eastern tropical Pacific and shifts rainfall
La Nina cools the same region and can intensify droughts
ENSO cycles occur roughly every two to seven years

faq.question: How does El Nino affect global weather?
faq.answer: El Nino weakens the trade winds, letting warm water spread east across the Pacific. This shifts the jet stream, bringing heavy rains to South America's west coast, drought to Australia and Southeast Asia, and milder winters to northern North America.

faq.question: Is climate change making El Nino events stronger?
faq.answer: Research suggests that warming may increase the frequency of extreme El Nino events. Warmer baseline ocean temperatures give each event more energy, potentially amplifying associated floods and heatwaves worldwide.
